pages.transcription:
c/o Viking Press
18 East 48th Street
New York

Ossining, July 19th, 1941

Dear Hanna, We had today your long letter of July 8th
and are very happy to know you in good spirits,
probably even happier now that Manfred is with you
after his successful exam. None of us doubted of course
that he would be successful, nevertheless we were glad
to get the confirmation and to hear that he is resting
in Bath. I hope that Marks managed to get really
good photos of you and Manfred for I must confess
that I don't like those which Eva has. I don't know
whether you are allowed to send snapshots of Rosemount.
It would be lovely to have them, too, although I still
have every detail in mind very clearly, and especially in
the month of June every day another event came back to
my mind very sharply. I may even allow myself to confess
just once that moments of acute homesickness occur
from time to time and that Miss Baker's idea of
returning for the school holidays was not bad at all,
if rather naïve in present times. - We are leading
a very quiet life here in the country, disturbed
only by world events and the ever acute question,
where to go and what to do next. I used to like
decisions at short notice, but nowadays this is
rather inconvenient. - It is nice to be near Eva,
and were we not so handicapped by being without
a car and therefore a misance to all who have one
we would go to see her still more often. I spent an
afternoon at Amity Hall last week, had supper there,
and Eva was allowed to stay up much longer, and
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte blau/violett. Sehr gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
to accompany Mrs. Sch. who drove me home. It was still
more thrilling for her because Mrs. Sch. showed me
the new house they are going to take from September
and Eva was the first child to see it. It is really
a most beautiful place, a big old Tudor house,
situated high on a hill with glorious views on the
Hudson, large grounds and as Eva said "just made
for Amity Hall" and nearly as beautiful as Rose-
mount. She is thoroughly enjoying the holiday,
they are kept busy with games and sports, go swimming,
play tennis etc, sleep in tents (next to the house)
and there are a few more girls in her age now.
You need not fear that she has outgrown all her
things. I had her summer dresses lengthened in spring
and they still fit her. Besides I got her one or two
cotton dresses for the garden which are very cheap,
and I don't think she needs anything until winter.
I shall talk it over with her and Mrs. Sch, however,
and write you what she could use for the winter.
As regards your questions about my housekeeping
I am sorry to have to disappoint you because I
got a white and not a colored maid. She is neat
and efficient and knows plain cooking, and she
gave me some excitement by disappearing for two
days on account of complicated love affairs. She came
back, however, and my landlady came and talked
to her about the moral side of the matter until she re-
pented and promised never to let me down again and
to conduct her own affairs strictly during her time off.

pages.transcription:
2)
I am glad that the Rosemount garden supplies you
with lots of fresh vegetables and fruit and I hope that also
the chickens do their duty. I am sure Mr. Miller keeps them
as fit and happy as he can. I hope that Marta can have
a good long holiday in Bath, and it will seem strange
to her to return as a guest into a house where she
belonged from the beginning. Victor, too, would cer-
tainly be happy to come back for a while. We were glad
to hear that Manfred seems satisfied with his state of
health, he wrote otherwise and his letters were very sad.
This last year has certainly mixed us up thoroughly,
and it would have seemed phantastic a year ago when
we had just arrived that now I am keeping house
in Ossining that Fuelop-Miller's would come over in
the evening and Stefan read them a chapter from his
autobiography, that Eva would live a few miles
away, and that Jules Romains and other people whom
we had not expected to see for years to come would
come out here to visit us. My hope is that just as
phantastically fast the changes for the good will
come before we dare to expect it. It is a rather
difficult moment for us now, because we do
not know and are yet unable to decide whether to
remain here, whether to leave the States and come
back later or whether to return to Brazil. This un-
certainty and all the problems involved with the
decision are a little hard on the nerves and Stefan
feels it more strongly than I do. It makes him work
more and more intensely and that keeps me busy.
The good thing is that since a few weeks I feel
quite well again and that the treatment finally
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte blau/violett. Sehr gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
seems to take effect. I had rather strong reactions for a
time temperature and even asthma attacks, and that pro-
bably accounts for my being a little thinner. But I
feel well now and have again learned to appreciate
consciously physical fitness. I still get my injections
of dust and bacterias once a week and go to New York
for that. At the same occasion I take Eva to the
dentist (she will be finished next time) and I also showed
my doctor a wart which Eva had developed and which
has meanwhile been removed. At this occasion my doctor's
wife who is orthopedist, gave Eva some exercises against
her tendency for flat-footedness, and if she is clever she
can turn these exercises into games with the others,
picking up marbles from the floor and writing with
the feet.
I hope that the Wilmot business is now
settled satisfactorily and we feel terribly sorry that you
who cannot know all our affairs should have to
work them out. Whatever new questions may unexpectedly
arise, please don't let them worry you, just remember
that you could not possibly know about everything and
that everything can be cleared up eventually. Wilmot
certainly is hard to know at first and it takes some time
to discover that while he seems to sit and hardly listen
to you, he is in reality thinking hard and trying to
help.
Have a good rest and holiday, both of
you and give my kindest regards to all. I
am so glad your brother found some decent work
at last.
Love and kisses,
Lotte
